messages.body_plain:
Hi Leonardo, thanks for the reply to my inquiry.

I guess in simplifying my example, I obscured what I am trying to do.
I want two layers (hence two dataframes). One has points and the other
has rectangles. However, whenever I use geom_rect with its own
dataframe that is different from the plot dataframe, which should be
possible from examples I've seen, I get an error like the example in
my note.

So I must not understand how ggplot2 determines aesthetics. I thought
geom_rect was looking for xmin, xmax, ymin and ymax, but NOT x or y.
The former might mapped to a variable in a call to aes(), but they
could also be set to particular values (i.e., not mapped), as in my
example, in which case they wouldn't need to be in aes(). So I'm not
sure what you mean when you say "Geom_rect needs an aesthetic and
you've specified it to have x=a". As far as I can tell from the
documentation, geom_rect doesn't need x. Correct me if I'm wrong.

David

messages.body_plain:
Brandon,

Thanks for your reply. But the problem is not so easily avoidable,
given what I want to do. See below.

David

On Dec 31, 2010, at 2:02 PM, Brandon Hurr wrote:

I guess when it is trying to define the x and y axis it is using the a
and b from the aes() call in the ggplot() call as reference, but when
you then use a different data for your geom_rect() layer it doesn't
know what to do.

If you switch df2 and df1 like below the code works without error so
it is clearly the lack of an a and b value in your df2 dataframe. That
being said, geom_rect() does not require an x or y in the aes() call
as you noted. It does seem slightly inconsistent but easily
avoidable.

df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
ggplot(data = df2, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
               data = df1,
               xmin = 0,
               xmax = 1,
               ymin = 0,
               ymax = 1)

Yes, but If I now try to use df1, I get a similar error:
==============================

df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
ggplot(data = df2, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
		data = df1,
		xmin = 0,
		xmax = 1,
		ymin = 0,

		ymax = 1) +
geom_point(colour = "red")
==============================

> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
> df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
> ggplot(data = df2, aes(x = a, y = b)) +

+ geom_rect(
+ 		data = df1,

+ 		xmin = 0,
+ 		xmax = 1,
+ 		ymin = 0,

+ 		ymax = 1) +
+ geom_point(colour = "red")

Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a' not found

I think the more important question would be why are you wanting to
reference one dataframe and then supply geom_rect() another? If you
have more than one dataframe to reference then you will likely have
another layer to plot. Best thing to do is to supply each layer
individually with "data=df, aes(x=x, y=y,...)" to avoid confusion for
you and the program.

I want to reference two dataframes because I want two layers in my
graph, one with points and other with rectangles. I eliminated one
layer (the one with points) to simplify the example but perhaps that
was confusing. In any case, I don't see how supplying each layer with
"data=df, aes(x=x, y=y,...)" helps because geom_rect doesn't want an x
and y, but rather xmin, xmax, ymin, and ymax.

HTH,

Brandon

messages.subject: Re: confused about geom_rect
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

On Fri, Dec 31, 2010 at 9:09 AM, David Fay <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Can anyone tell me why this works:
> ==============================
> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
> df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
> geom_rect(
>                xmin = 0,
>                xmax = 1,
>                ymin = 0,
>                ymax = 1)
> ==============================

It works because you established a coordinate system for the plot by defining a for x and b for y relative to df1. Once that coordinate system is established, it can determine xmin, xmax, ymin and ymax because it has a reference system with which to work. Since you provided no new data frame, by default geom_rect() will refer to the coordinate system set up in the ggplot() call; specifically, the use of a as the x-variable and b as the y-variable.

>
> but this doesn't (adding data parameter to geom_rect):
> ==============================
> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)
> df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)
> ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
> geom_rect(
>                data = df2,
>                xmin = 0,
>                xmax = 1,
>                ymin = 0,
>                ymax = 1)
> ==============================

In this snippet, you defined a coordinate system using a as the x-variable and b as the y-variable in the first line with respect to df1. Consequently, ggplot() assumes that variables a and b correspond to the x and y variables in subsequent layers *unless explicitly overwritten*. Since a and b do not exist in df2, you get the error message as shown below. This is a common 'gotcha' in ggplot2 and is worth remembering when using multiple data frames to construct a plot...been there :)

*Every* statement in a ggplot() call is coordinated...it takes a while to fully grasp this concept.

>
> > ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
> + geom_rect(
> +               data = df2,
> +               xmin = 0,
> +               xmax = 1,
> +               ymin = 0,
> +               ymax = 1)
> Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'a' not found
>

To illustrate my point, this works:

ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
 geom_rect(
                data = df2,

                aes(x = aa, y = bb),

                xmin = 0,
                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,
                ymax = 1)

Notice the redefinition of x and y as aesthetics to conform to the variables in df2 not common to df1.

This also works:

df2 <- df1              # df2 now has same variables as df1

ggplot(data = df1, aes(x = a, y = b)) +
geom_rect(
                data = df2,
                xmin = 0,
                xmax = 1,
                ymin = 0,
                ymax = 1)

 As does this:

df2 <- data.frame(aa = 1, bb = 1)

ggplot() + geom_rect(
                 data = df2,
                 aes(x = aa, y = bb),

                 xmin = 0,
                 xmax = 1,
                 ymin = 0,
                 ymax = 1)

This last approach is often useful if you know that you will be creating multiple layers in a plot using different variables with different names. Under this approach, all of the necessary aesthetics must be defined within the geom.

> Disregard the fact that I'm not using the dataframes for anything in
> my example. I plan to use them if I can.

Which is why I raised the last approach, in the hope it may come in handy for you...

Dennis

Hi:

On Fri, Dec 31, 2010 at 7:55 PM, David Fay <david...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks Dennis, that's very helpful.
>
> In fact, I was assuming that "*Every* statement in a ggplot() call is coordinated". In particular, I was assuming that since geom_rect needs an xmin and therefore also needs an x, it would look for it first in df2 (which it apparently does do) but then, not finding it, would look in df1, which it apparently does not do. So the statements are not very well coordinated, or at least in the way I was assuming.
>
> So, here's my question: if I want to plot points in one layer and (positionally independent) rectangles in a different layer, what's the best way to set up two data frames for this?My approach was to put the coordinates for the points in one data frame (two for each) and the coordinates for the rectangles in the other (four for each), but that doesn't work.

When I confront this problem, and I have a few times, I try to define the coordinates of rectangles in terms of an established x-y coordinate system, which may require that I add variables to the data frame of the rectangle(s) corresponding to those that define the (x, y) aesthetics in the ggplot() call. I do that to minimize headache inducement and BP spikes.

> By experimenting based on your tips, here's what I came up with:

>
>
> df1 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1)

> df2 <- data.frame(a = 1, b = 1, c = c(1, 2), d = c(1, 2))

>
> ggplot() +
> geom_rect(
>                data = df2,
>                aes(

>                        xmin = c - 1,
>                        xmax = c + 1,
>                        ymin = d - 1,
>                        ymax = d + 1
>                )
> ) +
> geom_point(
>                data = df1,
>                aes(x = a, y = b),
>                colour = "red"
> )
>

Yes, but what did you define as the x and y aesthetics in geom_rect()? Nothing was set with the ggplot() call nor in the geom_rect() call. When the argument to ggplot() is empty, all aesthetics have to be mapped *within each geom*. You did that in your call, but the aesthetics defined in geom_rect() are relative to df2 whereas the aesthetics defined in geom_point() are relative to df1. If you hadn't put in the geom_point() code, ggplot() would have had to construct the axis and coordinate system from the information it had available, which would have been from (xmin, xmax) and (ymin, ymax).  [And it actually works - I tried it :-] If you look at the on-line help page of geom_rect(), you'll see that x and y are not required inputs per se....

Here's another example for your consideration:

df4 <- data.frame(g = c(1, 2), h = c(1, 2))

ggplot() +
    geom_rect(
               data = df2,
               aes(

                       xmin = c - 1,
                       xmax = c + 1,
                       ymin = d - 1,
                       ymax = d + 1
                    )
             )  +
    geom_point(data = df4,
                        aes(x = g, y = h),
                        color = 'red',
                        size = 3
                      )

There are neither variables named g and h in df2 nor variables named c and d in df4, and yet it works :)  Which geom establishes the coordinate system?

> This works, but df2 is:
>
> > df2
>  a b c d
> 1 1 1 1 1
> 2 1 1 2 2
>
> which means that the values of the a and b variables are meaningless. All they do is to signal geom_rect to use the same x and y as geom_point does.

The variables a and b in df2 are not meaningless, but they were never invoked into use in your geom_rect() example.
>
> While this works, there must be a more sensible way to do this.

Happy New Year!!
Dennis

PS: Thank you for providing readable spacing and line breaks in your code. I hope it inspires others to try the same (hint! :)
>
> David

Geom rect neither requires nor uses x and y aesthetics, but if you
supply them they must exist. You could argue this is a bug, but it's a
pretty minor one.

Hadley

messages.subject: Re: confused about alpha
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The previous post was incorrect.
ggplot2 uses scale system for alpha, and by default, the alpha is
mapped to the range of 0.1-1.0.
see ?scale_alpha

This means that your transparency: 1/c(1, 128, 256, 32, 64, 96)
is mapped to the value:  1.0000000 0.1035294 0.1000000 0.1247059
0.1105882 0.1058824

The difference among 1/32, 1/64, etc is very very small, which fails
to enter our visual awareness.

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

The University of  Tokyo, Japan.

messages.body_plain:
I am wanting to form some (or all) of my arguments to qplot dynamically based on user input at the command line. I am dynamically generating the data set (query_results) from a database call and the string definition of main (title_str) based on the command line arguments. I could have several forms of qplot with various forms of the facet parameter and without it but I would be cleaner to generate this dynamically.

For example, at different times I need the following forms:
qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = sex ~ colony,
    main = title_str)

qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = . ~ colony,
    main = title_str)

qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = sex ~ species,
    main = title_str)

qplot(age, data = query_results, geom="histogram", # no facet parameter wanted
    binwidth = 1,
    main = title_str)

Mark

R. Mark Sharp, Ph.D.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mark,

I am a little unclear what your exact context is, but is this
something like what you want?

########################
foo <- function() {
  require(ggplot2)

  cat("Please type desired formula", fill = TRUE)
  f <- scan(file = "", what = "character", nlines = 1, sep = "\t")
  if (identical(length(f), 0L)) {
    f <- . ~ .
  } else {
    f <- as.formula(f)
  }

  qplot(x = Sepal.Length, data = iris, geom = "histogram",
    binwidth = 1, facets = f,
    main = "My Title")
}
#########################

The logical test of f is probably rather unreliable, but you could use
the function like:

## use default, no facets
> foo()
Please type desired formula
1:
Read 0 items

## use facets
> foo()
Please type desired formula
1: . ~ Species
Read 1 item

It might help if you could give a little more information about what
your exact problem is (e.g., reading in data from the console, passing
strings as arguments, ....).

Cheers,

Josh

TRUE, otherwise leave it as FALSE.  I put it as an argument here, but
you could set the variable however you decide (e.g., whether there is

  f <- . ~ .

    f <- as.formula(f)
  }

messages.body_plain:
Mark,

I am glad to hear it.  When you get a chance, I think the qplot code
will help you.  One of the nice features of ggplot2 is that it is
flexible, and one of the ways it does this is building up graphs piece
by piece.  Thus it is possible to do:

plot <- ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width))

if (some condition) {
  plot <- plot + geom_point()
}

if (some other condition) {
  plot <- plot + facet_grid(. ~ Species)
}

if (more conditions) {
  plot <- plot + geom_line()
}

print(plot)

If all the conditions were true, this would be equivalent (roughly) to:

ggplot(data = iris, aes(x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ Species) +
  geom_line()

or in qplot() terms (again roughly):

qplot(data = iris, x = Sepal.Length, y = Sepal.Width, facet = . ~
Species, geom = c("point", "line")).  The "plot" object can be added
to or not, and then when you are all done (or at intermediary steps),
the final thing can be printed to the graphics device.  This makes it
very easy to pick and choose what elements you want without having to
change much.

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: How can I fill points with black / white depending on the sign of the data?
messages.subject_clean: How can I fill points with black / white depending on the sign of the data?
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to figure out a nice way to plot some sensitivity
statistics (vector 'a', below) that have both positive and negative
values. Because of their distribution, it would be more clear to
present them on a log-scale, e.g. the log(abs()).

I would like to use either filled(+) or empty(-) circles to indicate
sign, but am not sure how to do this without making separate calls to
geom_point*() and I would like to learn if there is a way to do this
with a single call.

Here is some example data:

a <- c(-100, 1, -4, 30)

and a plot

ggplot() + geom_pointrange(aes(1:4, log(abs(a)),
                                              ymin=0,
ymax=log(abs(a))),
                                              shape = 21, fill =
'black')

but I would like to replace 'black' with "ifelse(a<0,'white','black')"

Thanks,

David

On 11-01-04 03:36 PM, David L wrote:
> I am trying to figure out a nice way to plot some sensitivity
> statistics (vector 'a', below) that have both positive and negative
> values. Because of their distribution, it would be more clear to
> present them on a log-scale, e.g. the log(abs()).
>
> I would like to use either filled(+) or empty(-) circles to indicate
> sign, but am not sure how to do this without making separate calls to
> geom_point*() and I would like to learn if there is a way to do this
> with a single call.

  How about:

library(ggplot2)

a <- c(-100, 1, -4, 30)

d <- data.frame(x=1:4,a)
ggplot(d) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(x=x, y=log(abs(a)),
                      ymin=0,ymax=log(abs(a)),
                      fill=factor(a<0),
                  shape=21))+
  scale_fill_manual(value=c("black","white"))

messages.subject: Re: Line types / legend
messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc,

Hopefully Hadley cleared things up, but just in case (if rather late):

d1 <- data.frame(x1=rnorm(100,4,.75))
d2 <- data.frame(x2=rnorm(100,3,.45))

library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot()
p + geom_density(data = d1, aes(x = x1, colour = "Set 1", linetype = "Set 1")) +
  geom_density(data = d2, aes(x = x2, colour = "Set 2", linetype = "Set 2")) +

  scale_x_continuous(limits=c(0,10), breaks=seq(0,10,.5))             +
  labs(x="X-axis Label", y="Y-axis Label")                            +

  scale_colour_manual(name = "Data Source", values = c("Set 1" =
"purple", "Set 2" = "black"))+
  scale_linetype_manual(name = "Data Source", values = c("Set 1" =
"solid", "Set 2" = "dashed")) +

  opts(title="Plot Title Here",
    plot.title=theme_text(size=15,face="bold"),
    panel.grid.minor=theme_blank(), panel.grid.major=theme_blank(),
    panel.background=theme_blank(), axis.line=theme_segment(),
    legend.key=theme_blank())

Don't forget to include the name for both scales if you want a
simplified legend and put the linetype argument inside aes().

HTH,

Josh

messages.subject: Re: Context for citing ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
Dear David,

On 01/06/2011 04:15 AM, David L wrote:
> Regarding 'ways to support ggplot2' https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/wiki/Ways-to-support-ggplot2
>
> Using citation("ggplot2") gives the citation information, and I would
> like to support the project in this way, but given that the tool used
> to plot my results is not directly related to the science at hand, it
> is not clear how exactly to cite ggplot in the text, except perhaps in
> the acknowledgements.
>
> Any suggestions or examples?
>

I'm currently preparing a manuscript where the respective information
(in LaTeX) reads:
...
All further data processing was done in the statistical environment
R\cite{R}, using the package
  ggplot2\cite{ggplot2} for graphical display.

\paragraph{Pre-processing.~}
The spectra were imported into the spectra handling package
hyperSpec\cite{hyperSpec} using
R.matlab\cite{R.matlab}.  The spectral ranges below 755\rcm and between
1850 and 2500\rcm were
discarded. Co-additions were multiplicatively signal corrected (package
pls\cite{Mevik2007}) and
...

We chemists are usually giving very detailed descriptions, much more
detailed than it is e.g. customary in many fields of physics. If this
detailed citation scheme is uncommon in your field, it should be
possible to include a summary sentence like
All data processing was done in the statistical environment R\cite{R},
using the packages
  \cite{long, list, of, all, used, packages}.

I have a bunch of automatic citation and .bib file generation functions,
which you can find towards the end of my helper file for package
vignettes
(http://r-forge.r-project.org/scm/viewvc.php/Vignettes/vignettes.defs?view=markup&root=hyperspec).
They are particularly useful for Sweave documents (for usage examples,
see e.g. the end of the vignette .Rnws in Vignettes/plotting/ and
Vignettes/laser/).

HTH

Claudia

messages.subject: Re: Context for citing ggplot?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

There are quite a lot of papers citing statistical software used in
their analyses,
e.g., see:
http://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=%22analyses+were+conducted+using+R%22+OR+%22analyses+were+conducted+using+SPSS%22

I think it is possible and reasonable to include the visualization
tool, so how about like this:

"The statistical analyses and visualization were conducted using R
2.12.1 [1] and ggplot2 8.9.0 [2]."

please fix my poor English ;-)

Why I think visualization tool can be included in the citation along
with the analyses software:
IMHO, visualization is getting more and more important in scientific
investigation.
Large and/or complicated data cannot be understood without
visualization from diverse aspects.
So, in a sense, visualization may be more than just plotting after
analyses, and be a part of analyses that enables to deeply inspect
data.
ggplot2 kindly helps me to work with the routine of inspecting data.
This is why I like and need ggplot2.

However, please note that I'm not sure that everyone, including
editors and reviewers, will agree to citing visualization tools.

HTH,

kohske

--

messages.subject_clean: plot width in mm plus grid.text axis labels in Times + font size of 9pt (???)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I‘m currently trying to submit an article to a journal where text in graphs has to be in Times New Roman, font size 9pt, when squeezed into the width of a column of 84mm. I would be most grateful if anybody could help me please. Unfortunately, I have prepared my graphs, one of which I attached as a PDF, without any set dimensions. I have tried to find out how to change font type and size in grid.text, and how to define the width of the plot, but wasn’t successful. I have attached the same graph as an R-script as well but if someone wants to have a brief look at my current problem I also pasted it in below.

Best wishes and many thanks in advance,

Martin

rm(list=ls())

library(proto)

library(grid)

library(reshape)

library(plyr)

library(digest)

library(ggplot2)

df.perc.2 <- structure(list(trt = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L), class = "factor", .Label = c("0-1", "1-2", "2-3")),

                resp = c(100, 94.0193416337148, 90.4454585871723,

                               100, 97.865467535666, 95.8563947267053),

                group = structure(c(2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label = c("eggs in worker cells", "eggs in drone cells"), class = "factor"),

                se = c(0, 1.68994661360938, 2.95728999211006,

                               0, 0.549126551165786, 0.824844616926236)),

                .Names = c("trt", "resp", "group", "se"), row.names = c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# Currently, I'm saving plots in this way. However, I'm open for better suggestions:

# pdf("C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\\nur.fueR\\cost of worker policing project analysis_part 1\\Graphiken in ggplot2\\PDFs, PNGs\\A.plot5h.pdf")

# Is it possible to change the format of this graph to a witdh of 84mm when printed in a journal without messing up the graph completely?

ggplot(df.perc.2, aes(y = resp, x = trt, group = group, colour = group, linetype = group)) +

                scale_colour_manual(values = c("#000000", "#000000")) +

                geom_smooth(aes(ymax = resp + se, ymin = resp - se), data = df.perc.2, stat = "identity", size = 1) +

                opts(legend.position = c(0.38, 0.313), legend.background = theme_rect(colour = 0)) +

                opts(legend.key = theme_rect(colour = 0)) +

                opts(legend.title = theme_blank()) +

                opts(legend.text = theme_text(size = 20)) +

                scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.05), name = "") + scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.02, 0), breaks = seq(90, 100, 5), name = "") +

                opts(axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 20, vjust = 1), axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 20, hjust = 1)) +

                opts(plot.margin = unit(c(1.1, 1, 2, 1.2), "lines"))

                grid.text("age range of eggs [day]", x = unit(0.555, "npc"), y = unit(0.05, "npc"), gp=gpar(fontsize = 27))

                grid.text("eggs remaining [%]", x = unit(0.04, "npc"), y = unit(0.55, "npc"), rot = 90, gp=gpar(fontsize = 27))

# Alas, the journal where I would like to submit the manuscript including this graph also want's the text in Times and for the font size 9pt.

# The problem  now is that, as far as I know, grid.text is not part of ggplot and I don't know how to change font type and size in grid.text.

# Also, how would one change the font type and size for the ggplot function (e.g. for the axis.text)?

# dev.off()

                .Names = c("trt", "resp", "group", "se"), row.names =
c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

p = ggplot(df.perc.2) + theme_bw(9) +
  geom_smooth(aes(y = resp, x = trt, linetype = group, group=group,

                  ymax = resp + se, ymin = resp - se),

              stat = "identity", size = 1, colour="black") +
  opts(legend.position = c(0.5, 0.3),
       legend.background = theme_rect(colour = NA),
       legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA),
       legend.title = theme_blank(),
       legend.text = theme_text(size = 9),

       axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 9, hjust = 0.6,angle=90),
       axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 9, hjust = 1),
       plot.margin = unit(c(0.1,0.2,0,0), "lines")) +
  scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.05),
                   name = "age range of eggs [day]") +

  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.02, 0), breaks = seq(90, 100, 5),

##p

## 0.5047123 0.3111111

g <- ggplotGrob(p)

pdf("test.pdf",width=8.4/2.54, height=8.4/2.54)
grid.draw(editGrob(g, gPath( "text"), grep=TRUE,global=TRUE,
           gp=gpar(fontfamily="Times")))
dev.off()

HTH,

baptiste

         pointsize = 9, useDingbats = FALSE)

HTH,
Dennis

Hi Martin,

This is not  as precise as your plot, but I don’t know of any other way of taking advantage of ggsave scaling option. The other options would be using ‘pdf’ as you already do but adjusting font sizes …

On the other hand, you can use inkscape <http://inkscape.org/> to make this kind of final adjustments (by the way, font size 9 for every element in the plot? … I would not take this too serious).

Hope this helps, all the best,

fernando

Hi again:

I got what seems to be equivalent to Baptiste's graph as follows:

df.perc.2 <- structure(list(trt = structure(c(1L, 2L, 3L, 1L, 2L, 3L),
class = "factor", .Label = c("0-1", "1-2", "2-3")),
               resp = c(100, 94.0193416337148, 90.4454585871723,
                              100, 97.865467535666, 95.8563947267053),
               group = structure(c(2L, 2L, 2L, 1L, 1L, 1L), .Label =
c("eggs in worker cells", "eggs in drone cells"), class = "factor"),
               se = c(0, 1.68994661360938, 2.95728999211006,
                              0, 0.549126551165786, 0.824844616926236)),
               .Names = c("trt", "resp", "group", "se"), row.names =
c(NA, -6L), class = "data.frame")

# Incorporating Baptiste's use of theme_bw(),

q = ggplot(df.perc.2) + theme_bw(base_size = 9) +

 geom_smooth(aes(y = resp, x = trt, linetype = group, group=group,

                 ymax = resp + se, ymin = resp - se),

             stat = "identity", size = 1, colour="black") +
 opts(legend.position = c(0.5, 0.3),
      legend.background = theme_rect(colour = NA),
      legend.key = theme_rect(colour = NA),
      legend.title = theme_blank(),

      axis.title.x = theme_text(hjust = 0.6),
      axis.title.y = theme_text(hjust = 0.6, angle=90),
      axis.text.y = theme_text(hjust = 1),
      plot.margin = unit(c(0.1,0.2,0,0), "lines")) +
 scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.05),
                  name = "age range of eggs [day]") +

 scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.02, 0), breaks = seq(90, 100, 5),

                    name = "eggs remaining [%]")

ggsave(q, file = 'mytest.pdf', width = 3.3, height = 3.3, family = 'Times')

It's interesting that the base_size = parameter of theme_bw() worked on the opts() but not the base_family = parameter. I tried using base_family = 'Times' in theme_bw() to no avail, but Plan B, using the family = argument of pdf() in the ggsave() call, did work, so no harm.

Dennis

messages.subject: Re: plot width in mm plus grid.text axis labels in Times + font size of 9pt (???)
messages.subject_clean: plot width in mm plus grid.text axis labels in Times + font size of 9pt (???)
messages.body_plain:
Hi, here is my solution. This is almost same as Baptiste's one, except
for the method creating pdf.

p <- ggplot(df.perc.2, aes(y = resp, x = trt, group = group, linetype
= group)) +

                geom_smooth(aes(ymax = resp + se, ymin = resp - se),

colour = "black", stat = "identity", size = 1) +

                scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.05), name = "age
range of eggs [day]") +
                scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0.02, 0), breaks =

seq(90, 100, 5), name = "eggs remaining [%]") +
                opts(legend.position = c(0.4, 0.22),
                        legend.background = theme_blank(),
                        legend.key = theme_blank(),

                        legend.title = theme_blank(),
                        legend.text = theme_text(size = 9),

                        axis.text.x = theme_text(size = 9, vjust = 1),
                        axis.text.y = theme_text(size = 9, hjust = 1),
                        axis.title.x = theme_text(size = 9),
                        axis.title.y = theme_text(size = 9, angle = 90))

width = as.numeric(convertUnit(unit(84, "mm"), "inch"))
height = as.numeric(convertUnit(unit(96, "mm"), "inch"))

ggsave("plot.pdf", p, width = width, height = height, family = "Times")

to Dennis:

>It's interesting that the base_size = parameter of theme_bw() worked on the opts() but not the base_family = parameter. I tried using base_family = 'Times' in theme_bw() to no avail, but Plan B, using the family = argument of pdf() in the ggsave() call, did work, so no harm.

base_size and base_family should work similarly.
What is confusing is the default size in theme_text is 10, which is
very similar to the size specified in base_size.
If any text elements are specified in opts() using theme_text(), then
any global setting are overwritten.
So, try this code:

r <- qplot(1:2, 1:2) + theme_grey(base_size=20, base_family="Times") +
 opts(axis.title.x = theme_text(colour="red")) +
 labs(x = "size = 9, family = default of the device",
      y = "size = 20, family = Times")

ggsave("test.png")
ggsave("test.pdf")

--
Kohske Takahashi <takahash...@gmail.com>

Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology,
The University of  Tokyo, Japan.
http://www.fennel.rcast.u-tokyo.ac.jp/profilee_ktakahashi.html

messages.body_plain:
Hi Kohske:

KT: "If any text elements are specified in opts() using theme_text(), then

any global setting[s] are overwritten."

I had actually observed this while fooling around with Baptiste's code - the base_family = 'Times' font worked on the legend text where no opts() command was available, but for any opts() statement in the plot call that involved theme_text() with some overwriting argument, the font would revert back to Helvetica. Thank you for the explanation - very illuminating. I agree that the font sizes were too close for me to discriminate - your example clarified the issue, so now I understand better why Baptiste's solution is preferable in that regard.

Thanks to both you and Baptiste for teaching me a few new things about ggplot2 and grid today :)

Best regards,
Dennis

My apologies for the delayed reply. After sending you my previous
question I travelled back to the UK (from Austria) which took me some
time.

Thank you for your various solutions which all seem to solve the
problem. I am very grateful for that. Only problem: I never used
ggsave() until now, apparently a mistake ;-), and I cannot get it
working on my laptop. I know that’s a bit embarrassing but I always
get an error message. The most common one reads:

Error in pdf("test.pdf", width = 8.4/2.54, height = 8.4/2.54) :
  file 'test.pdf' cannot be opened

I checked all sorts of things but I haven’t found out why it does not
work. I have attached my session info at the end of the message in
case this explains it. Also, one thing I don’t understand: If it
works, where does ggsave() actually save the plots?

Best wishes,

Martin

If you don't specify a directory it will put it in your R working directory. On my mac it puts them in my user folder, on a PC... I'm not sure. Make a file with a very unique name and search for it.

-B

messages.body_plain:
getwd() will tell you where the file is saved; setwd() allows you to
specify the working directory. I don't know what the problem is (file
permissions, perhaps), but it seems likely that it has nothing to do
with ggplot2 per se. Try with this example,

pdf("newTestFile.pdf")
plot(1,1)
dev.off()

and if this fails my suggestion would be to ask on R-help.

HTH,

baptiste

Dear Brandon and Baptiste,

Thank you two for helping me with this ggsave() issue. I followed all
your suggestions. I then also read in an R book and on the internet
(and even reinstalled R which didn’t help either). The strange thing
is that
setwd(file = "C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\\nur.fueR\\ggsave\\")
does not work (from the book and it used to work), whilst
setwd("C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\\nur.fueR\\ggsave\\")
does work (by chance from the internet). (I checked it using the
newTestFile.pdf from Baptiste and this works.)

Anyway, my laptop either does not have a default R working directory
or it must be broken. Before deleting my previous R version getwd()
gave me
[1] "C:/Windows/system32" (pretty shocking, I know ;-)
After installing the new R version I received
[1] "C:/Users/mhk/Documents".
However, both didn’t work. To me this is really bizarre.

Fingers crossed I can now also save all ggsave examples that I
received. If ggsave keeps on working I think this will be my favourite
way of saving things because it is much shorter and gives more options
of how to save things.

Best wishes,

Martin

messages.subject: Bug on position=dodge?
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

Ignore the format of the x-axis; this is just an example…

This works:

yr2<-c(2009,2009,2010,2010)

ri2<-c(10.231250, 6.460317, 11.7754, 5.453634)

fr2<-c("Eldorado","Inyo","Eldorado","Inyo")

data.df2<-as.data.frame(cbind(yr2,ri2,fr2), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

names(data.df2)<-c("year","richness","forest")

data.df2$year<-as.numeric(data.df2$year)

data.df2$richness<-as.numeric(data.df2$richness)

qqq<-ggplot(data.df2,aes(y=richness, x=year, linetype=forest, shape=forest))

qqq + geom_point(size=4, position="dodge")

This produces an error:

yr<-c(2009,2009)

ri<-c(10.231250, 6.460317)

fr<-c("Eldorado","Inyo")

data.df1<-as.data.frame(cbind(yr,ri,fr), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

data.df1$yr<-as.numeric(data.df1$yr)

data.df1$ri<-as.numeric(data.df1$ri)

names(data.df1)<-c("year","richness","forest")

data.df1$year<-as.numeric(data.df1$year)

data.df1$richness<-as.numeric(data.df1$richness)

qqq<-ggplot(data.df1,aes(y=richness, x=year, linetype=forest, shape=forest))

qqq + geom_point(size=4, position="dodge")

Error in if (any(diff(intervals) < -1e-06)) { :

  missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

But this works:

qqq + geom_point(size=4)

Cheers,

Leo

Dear Dennis and Brandon,

Thank you for your help. I have now checked again whether, without
setting a specific working directory, R really does not save graphs in
"C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\\". Alas, I was right. It really doesn’t
work, no matter whether I tried to save a graph as a pdf, png or jpg.
However, and now it starts getting really strange, when I manually
define it as the working directory, setwd("C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\
\"), I can suddenly save the graph as a pdf but not as a png or as a
jpg. I can also change the working directory to setwd("C:\\Users\\mhk\
\Documents\\nur.fueR\\ggsave\\") and get the same results.
Fortunately, I only want to use pdf anyway, otherwise it would be
annoying.

I’m using Windows 7 on a new Sony laptop. And yes, I have been
searching in "C:\\Users\\mhk\\Documents\\" and to make things even
more confusing I have one test file there which I cannot explain how
it got there because now it wouldn’t work anymore :-S.

But don’t worry for the moment since ggsave is working for a set
working directory, at least for pdfs. If you have any ideas which
other things I could try to tidy up this mess on my computer I would
be most grateful, however.

Best wishes,

Martin

p.s.: To Dennis: Thanks for these suggestions how to better organise
my R files. I will try to find out how to do it and if I need further
help contact you. It does sound very useful.

p.p.s.: If anyone knows about any reading material on ggsave(),
grid.draw(), grid.text() or the like I would be very grateful for any
suggestions. I have access to many journals of the Web of Knowledge,
in case this would be necessary. Also, I’m always happy to buy a good
book if need be.

messages.subject: Re: Bug on position=dodge?
messages.body_plain:
It is a bug.  You can see it with an even simpler example:

df1 <- data.frame(x=1, y=1)
ggplot(df1, aes(x=x, y=y)) + geom_point(position="dodge")

I've filed a bug report (and proposed patch): https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/issue/157

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University

messages.subject: Re: stat_summary question
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

To add to Kohske's comments, it also appears you want an average line; here's a toy example that shows how to do that as well, using group = 1 in conjunction with geom_smooth():

# Nine subjects in three treatment groups, each with responses on categories A-E
df <- data.frame(Treatment = factor(rep(1:3, each = 15)),
                 subj = rep(1:9, each = 5),
                 Category = rep(LETTERS[1:5], 9),
                 Response = rnorm(45))
p <- ggplot(df, aes(x = Category, y = Response, groups = subj, colour = Treatment))
p + geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line(size = 1) +
    geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), colour = 'black', se = FALSE, size = 2)

If you'd like confidence bands around the average line, use se = TRUE (the default). This idea is borrowed from the example on pp. 50-51 of Hadley's book and adapted to categorical x variables. The variable names were chosen to minimize code writing in the ggplot() call.

What if one wants average lines per treatment plus an overall average line? It's more convenient to produce the treatment averages in a separate data frame first, and it's actually better to produce a separate plot for this purpose:

library(plyr)
# Average Response over Treatment x Category combinations
dfavg <- ddply(df, .(Treatment, Category), summarise, Average = mean(Response))
# Redo above plot on new data frame
q <- ggplot(dfavg, aes(x = Category, y = Average, color = Treatment, group = Treatment))
q + geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line(size = 1) +
    geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), color = 'black', size = 1.5)

# ...or you could try this instead:
p + geom_point(size = 2.5) + geom_line(size = 1) +
    geom_smooth(aes(group = 1), colour = 'black', se = FALSE, size = 1) +
    facet_grid(Treatment ~ .)

It helps to know that when the x-variable is categorical, geom_smooth() will produce group averages as the default 'smooth', so you can avoid the use of stat_summary() for this purpose. Of course, there are other contexts in which stat_summary() may be the better choice.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: RE: Overplotting data from different files
messages.body_plain:
Dear Noble,

That is possible. But not by using ggplot() twice. Soppuse you want to
display the first file as points. Then the code would be

ggplot(file1,aes(deltat,deltam)) + geom_point()

If you want to add the second file as an extra layer of points then the
code would be

ggplot(file1,aes(deltat,deltam)) + geom_point() + geom_point(data =
file2)

So the trick is to add the extra geoms that you need and supply the new
dataframe with the data argument. Note that you can also change the
aesthetics if the names in the new dataframe are different.

ggplot(file1,aes(x = deltat, y = deltam)) + geom_point() +
geom_point(data = file2, aes(x = deltam, y = deltat))

Best regards,

Thierry

You can, yes (see solution 2 below), but it's more likely that you'll
rather want to combine the data beforehand.

## fake data sets organised in a list
my.data <- replicate(5,data.frame(x=1:10,y=rnorm(10)),simplify=FALSE)

names(my.data) <- paste("file",seq_along(my.data))
str(my.data)

## version 1, combine data.frames

m <- melt(my.data,id='x')
str(m)

ggplot(m) +
  geom_path(aes(x,value,colour=L1))

## version 2, using a loop to add layers

make.layer <- function(ii){
  geom_path(aes(x,y), data=my.data[[ii]], colour=ii)
}
all.layers <- llply(seq(2,length(my.data)), make.layer)

p.ini <- ggplot(my.data[[1]]) +
  geom_path(aes(x,y))

p.ini + all.layers

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
what brandon showed was for continuous variables, ie using scale_gradientn(). i only suggested discretizing since you originally used scale_manual(). look at scale_gradientn() for more details on including pre-defined colour pallettes, e.g.

conc20_cont + geom_tile(aes(fill=z)) + scale_fill_gradientn(colour=(rainbow(7)[7:1]))

What Brandon did (based on your original colours) matched your previous graph much better.

messages.subject: adding polygon to density surface
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have been making a plot which is a density surface and overlaying a transparency that represents error in the surface.  The higher the error the more transparent the plot.  I have done what I thought would be the hard part and made the plot but now I am having trouble adding a polygon to it.  The toy example below is a pretty course representation of what i have done but should give you an idea.  The polygons I have for the plots are coastlines and I may have several polygons per plot.

I also have two other questions detailed in the code below.  These are on switching the direction of the transparency scale and  changing the plot colour.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Many Thanks

Lindesay Scott-Hayward

# Toy example for ggplot
x = 1:20
y = 1:20

grid = expand.grid(x, y)

# function values
func = (grid[,1]^2)/1000

# error values to be added to the plot so that areas of high error are more transparent
knot = c(10,10)
errors = exp(-(sqrt(apply((grid-knot)^2, 1, sum))/1))

d = sqrt(apply((grid-knot)^2, 1, sum))

circ.err  = - d^2 * log (d)/100
circ.err[190] = 0
p = ggplot(grid, aes(grid[,1], grid[,2], fill = func, alpha = errors)) + geom_tile()
p
# the addition of transparency to represent errors works fine but I wonder is it possible to change the scale around so that 0 error is represented full colour (zero transparency) and maximum error represents maximum transparency (i.e. little colour showing on plot)

# polygon adding
pol = data.frame(x1 = c(12, 16, 16, 12), x2 = c(12, 12, 16, 16))
p + layer(geom = 'polygon', data=p1)

# this gives an error of differing lengths

# Lastly how do i change the colour of my plot.  I have tried

p = ggplot(grid, aes(grid[,1], grid[,2], fill = func, alpha = errors)) + geom_tile() + scale_colour_gradientn(colours = terrain.colors(100))
p
 # but it does not change the colour of my plot

messages.subject: Ordering facets?
messages.body_plain:
I think I get the idea, but I can't seem to make this work.  My data set
is large and my time is short (a few hours or less), so I hope someone has
a tip based on a description.  If necessary, I will try to generate an
example.

I have a dataframe in long format with US state abbreviations, data to
plot, year (almost a 50-year span), and measurement type.  I'm plotting
facet-wrapped graphs of data as a function of year for one specific
measurement type, with each facet containing the result for a specific
state.

In other words, the data structure looks sort of like

datum1 + datum2 + datum3 ~ year + state + type

if I remember ddply notation properly.

(I actually have several such graphs to produce, each plotting a different
data column.)

Instead of ordering facets based on alphabetical order of state
abbreviations, I'd like to order them based on a descending value of the
selected data column in a particular year.

The command to produce alphabetized plots looks something like

ggplot(dataframe,
       aes(x=Year,y=datacolumnname))+
  facet_wrap(~ StateAbbrev)+
  expand_limits(y=0)+
  geom_line()+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(1960,1980,2000))+
  scale_y_continuous("Data Column Name")

What do I change to sort by descending value of the data in a certain
year?  I know it has to do with reordering the StateAbbrev factor somehow.

Thanks,

Bill

messages.subject: Re: Error in geom_histogram
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

@ Trevor, you can get around this by specifying the binwidth argument.
 Given the huge values you are working with, I would use a large
number (e.g., 10^5) or it could take a long time.  Alternately, use
smaller numbers.

@ Dr. Bolker, thanks for the easy example.

I think this comes down to floating point precision issues for numbers
of this size in the default cutting/binning code.  The actual test is
in position-collide.r ~~ line 40.  Relaxing the test on the standard
deviation of the widths (xmax - xmin for each bar), also "fixes" the
problem.

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: Using Dates for Axes
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

I'm a relative new comer to the R and ggplot2 party (Python tends to
be my default language, but I've been envious of the ggplot2 images
I've seen, so I figured it was time to learn it.)

I have a set of data depicting the number of injuries and fatalities
resulting from January tornadoes.  I can create a plot that displays
both injuries and fatalities by year, however I'm simply treating the
year as an integer.  When I try to create the same plot treating the
year as POSIXct objects the x-axis has no x-ticks.  Any help on what
I'm doing wrong and tips for doing things better would be appreciated.

You can find the code here:  https://gist.github.com/783238

Patrick

messages.subject: Re: Using Dates for Axes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Patrick,

I think the tick mark issue has to do with a misnamed variable or
possibly the POSIX standard.  Unless you will later be dealing with
hours/minutes/seconds, just use the date class.

Everyone is a bit different and has their own style they prefer for
"doing things better".  One thing that comes to mind is you might want
to consider a y axis transformation or the little years get completely
overpowered.  Here's my take.

Cheers,

Josh

##########################

require(ggplot2)

jan <- structure(list(years = 1950:2009, Injuries = structure(c(15,
11, 15, 21, 2, 0, 12, 34, 17, 5, 4, 0, 31, 15, 10, 9, 0, 290,
0, 241, 7, 27, 147, 56, 28, 380, 9, 0, 46, 1, 1, 0, 36, 7, 0,
0, 0, 1, 93, 64, 37, 20, 2, 3, 8, 76, 58, 60, 10, 346, 22, 12,
0, 0, 3, 31, 41, 39, 52, 0), .Dim = 60L), Fatalities = structure(c(1,
0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 13, 0, 3, 0, 0, 1, 1, 10, 0, 0, 7, 0, 32, 0,
1, 5, 1, 2, 12, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 5, 0, 0,
1, 0, 0, 0, 3, 1, 2, 0, 18, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 4, 1, 2, 7, 0), .Dim = 60L)),
.Names = c("years", "Injuries", "Fatalities"),
row.names = c(NA, -60L), class = "data.frame")

jan$years <- as.Date(paste(jan$years, "-01-15", sep=""))
jan.melt <- melt(jan, measure.vars=c("Injuries", "Fatalities"))
colnames(jan.melt) <- c("Year", "Casualty", "Count")

xlabs <- scale_x_date(name = "Year", major = "5 years", minor = "1 year")
ylabs <- scale_y_continuous(name = "Count", trans = "sqrt")
leg <- opts(title="January Casualties by Year (1950-2009)",
  legend.position=c(0.2, 0.8), legend.background=theme_rect("white"))

## Original
## note the binwidth...dates are stored as numbers, as.Date() by days
## POSIX by seconds, I think, so adjust the binwidth accordingly
ggplot(jan.melt, aes(x = Year, fill = Casualty, weight = Count)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 365, position = 'dodge') +
  xlabs + ylabs + leg

## A bit of an alternative, I'm not in love with the lines but the
## offset bars distract me---injuries & fatalities happen at once
ggplot(jan.melt, aes(x = Year, y = Count, colour = Casualty)) +
  geom_line() +
  xlabs + ylabs + leg

  Hmmm. I had to tweak your code a bit to get it to run at all:

## next line fails in original form: changed X from '1:100' to '1:120'
t1 <-data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,1,each=60)),X = 1:120)

t1$Y1 <- runif(t1$X)
t1$Y2 <- runif(t1$X)*100000
t1 <-t1[,-2]
str(t1)

## why not:
t1 <- data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,each=60)),Y1=runif(120),
                 Y2=runif(120)*1e5)

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y1))
## next line was identical. Did you mean to plot Y2 instead?
ggplot(data=t1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=Y2))

m1 <-melt(t1, ids="n")

# ============

  The messages are not errors, they are warnings.
  I think what's happening is that you are asking R to plot 120 separate
rows, *one for each value of the data* (i.e. each histogram has a single
value in it).  Since ggplot is slow at faceting, this takes longer than
you are willing to wait.  Try

t2 <- data.frame(n=factor(rep(1:2,each=5)),Y1=runif(10),
                 Y2=runif(10)*1e5)
ggplot(data=melt(t2,ids="n"))+geom_histogram(aes(x=value))+facet_grid(value~.)

  Is this what you meant?  I think you might have preferred

## changed ggplot2 to ggplot
ggplot(data=m1)+geom_histogram(aes(x=value))+facet_grid(variable~.)

   I would consider it a bit of a limitation of ggplot2 (despite its
general wonderfulness) that it does not allow any simple way to set
non-default binwidths that are *different* in each facet.  Hadley would
probably say that this is a feature; faceting is designed to display
multiple subsets of the same data in small multiples.  What we are doing
here is an "off-label" (in the pharmaceutical sense) approach to fitting
multiple different variables, each in its own facet.  Since it conflicts
with the design philosophy of ggplot2, it's harder to achieve.

  cheers
    Ben Bolker

What you are doing here is asking for:

facets.  Is that really what you wanted or were you deliberately
trying to make it crash?

These are not errors, just notes from ggplot about what it is doing.
The reason there are so many is that you are faceting so many times.

>
> and then a consistent loss of control to R

ggplot2 is not the fastest thing ever, and you just asked it for 200
something histograms faceted into some monstrous display.  If you want
that, you'll need a powerful system and some patience.

Perhaps you meant:

ggplot(data = m1) + geom_histogram(aes(x = value)) +
  facet_grid(. ~ variable + n)

?  or some variant of that?

Josh

Just my personal opinion, but > 1 period in a variable (or really any
R object) is a stylistic and interpretability nightmare that seems
well worth the effort of preempting by:

A) Changing the naming scheme (if self created )
B) If it is the results of something automated (database query /
read.table with illegal characters) making renaming them the first
step

For example consider the headache of (particular the interaction term):

lm(Iris..2 ~ Iris......2 * Iris.....2, data = whatever)

Cheers,

Josh

messages.subject: adding a layer to qplot
messages.body_plain:
I submitted this as a bug, but it got rejected as being part of the
design.  What is the design behind this?

The first plot creates a quick plot of spatial data.  Works fine.

The second adds a layer for the geographic boundaries.  works just fine.

The third plot adds color and size mappings to the quick plot.  This
does not work.

The fourth is what I would assume is happening behind the scenes of
qplot+layer.  This works.

What It appears to me is that the x and y mappings are being retained
and correctly associated with the data dataset, but the associations
for color and size are being lost when adding a new layer since it is
looking for the color and size variables in the dataset for the new
layer.

---
library(maps)
library(ggplot2)
reg <- as.data.frame(map("county", "wyoming", plot = FALSE)[c("x", "y")])

data<-data.frame(
   rx=runif(100, -111.05,-104.05), #- Longitude    104°3'W to 111°3'W
   ry=runif(100,41,45), # - Latitude   41°N to 45°N
   rz=rnorm(100),
   rw=rnorm(100))

#works
qplot(rx,ry,col=rz, size=rw, data=data)

 #works
qplot(rx,ry, data=data)+layer(data=reg, mapping = aes(x=x,y=y), geom='path')

#does not work
last_plot()+layer(data=reg, mapping = aes(x=x,y=y), geom='path')

# works
ggplot()+
layer(geom='point', data=data, mapping=aes(x=rx,y=ry,color=rz, size=rw))+
layer(geom='path', data=reg, mapping=aes(x, y))
---

what  is going on here behind the scenes that I'm not understanding?

Thanks,
Andrew Redd

messages.subject: geom_hex() + coord_map(project) issue
messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure if this issue is known.  If it is how do I get around it?
 geom_hex only works with coord_map(project="cylindrical") which I
think is the default.  For any other value of the projection the hex
bins do not appear.

---
library(maps)
library(ggplot2)
WY <- qplot(x,y,data=as.data.frame(map("county", "wyoming", plot =
FALSE)[c("x", "y")]), geom='path')

data<-data.frame(
  rx=rnorm(1000, -108.05, sd=1), #- Longitude    104°3'W to 111°3'W
  ry=rnorm(1000,43, sd=.5)# - Latitude   41°N to 45°N
)

# works
WY+geom_point(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry))+coord_map(project="azequalarea")
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="cylindrical")

# does not work
# hex bins do not appear.
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="azequalarea")
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="gilbert")
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="lagrange")
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="orthographic")
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="conic", lat0=41)
WY+geom_hex(data=data, mapping=aes(rx,ry)) + coord_map(project="bonne", lat0=41)
---

Thanks,
Andrew

messages.subject_clean: Retaining legend icon size (visibility) when plot size gets small
messages.body_plain:
Hi all -

I was wondering if anyone knew an easy solution to this problem instead of the rig below.  The problem is fairly evident from the comments -

df <- data.frame(x = 1:5, y = 1:5)

# i want to be able to easily see the color in the legend in the below plot
# i.e., make the points in the legend big, while those in the plot are small
qplot(x, y, data = df, colour = x, size = I(1))

# this works...
ggplot(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = x, size = 1), data = df) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_size(legend = FALSE)

# ...but i need this construction...
ggplot() +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y, colour = x, size = 0*x+1), data = df) +
  scale_size(legend = FALSE)

# surely there's an easier way to do this? i.e., without creating a bogus
# function of one of the variables?

Ideas?

Thanks,
david.

Hi, perhaps these will be changed in the next version of ggplot2, but you can do it by:

TransLogrev <- Trans$new("logrev", function(x) -log(x), function(x) exp(-x), function(x) exp(-x))

d <- data.frame(x = rlnorm(1000))

p <- ggplot(d, aes(x)) + stat_density() +

  scale_x_continuous(trans="logrev")

print(p)

--

messages.subject: RE: adding polygon to density surface
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The trick is the following;

p = ggplot(grid, aes(grid[,1], grid[,2], fill = func, alpha = circ.err)) + geom_tile() +

scale_fill_gradientn(colours = topo.colors(100)) +

scale_alpha_continuous(to = c(0,1), trans = "reverse") +

theme_bw()

is the same as:

p = ggplot(data = grid, aes(x = grid[,1], y = grid[,2], fill = func, alpha = circ.err)) + geom_tile(aes(x = grid[,1], y = grid[,2], fill = func, alpha = circ.err)) …

so to simplify tha syntax, it assumes shared aesthetics are the same between geoms if the contrary is not specified.

In the case of the polygons you want to draw;

# polygon adding

pol = data.frame(Var1 = c(12, 16, 16, 12), Var2 = c(12, 12, 16, 16))

p + layer(geom = 'polygon', data=pol) == p + layer(geom = 'polygon', data=pol, aes(x = grid[,1], y = grid[,2], fill = func, alpha = circ.err)))

the strange thing is that you don’t receive an error … (that’s why I forwarded the email also to the ggplot2 list) .. even this syntax produces the same result:

p + layer(geom = 'polygon', data=pol, mapping = aes(x = grid[,1], y = grid[,2]))

in any case, it seems you need to overcome the default aesthetics to

p + layer (data = pol, geom = "polygon", mapping = aes(x = Var1, y = Var2), alpha = I(1), fill = I("grey20"))

p + geom_polygon(data = pol, aes(x = Var1, y = Var2), alpha = I(1), fill = I("pink"))

(by the way, I think this is the first or second time I use ‘layer’ to make a plot)

Hope this helps, all the best,

fernadno

messages.subject: RE: Boxplot attributes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Troy,

You can specify the attributes directly and not as aesthetics (in that case ggplot2 understands NULL and “blue” as the names of variables and takes default values for the fill and the colour)

Hope this helps,

fernando

library(ggplot2)

df <- data.frame(meas='x', val=1:10)

print(ggplot(df, aes(meas, val)) +

                geom_jitter()+geom_boxplot(fill=I(alpha("white", 0)), color=I("blue")))

messages.subject: Re: pattern fill
messages.body_plain:
I could see it being useful for those dreaded dynamite plots, but also geom_tile. If it could be made to work with geom_polygon & geom_area you could use it to pattern over an area of a map. I see its' main purpose as making graph objects distinctive in the absence of color or over the top of color. I would suggest that is perhaps it's sole purpose (primarily for publication reasons), although I'm sure others could come up with other reasons it could be useful to them.

B

messages.subject: geom_bar with multiple values for a category
messages.subject_clean: geom_bar with multiple values for a category
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have come across a situation where I want to do a bar plot grouped
by particular categories but some categories have more than one
value.  In this situation I would like two bars by each other.

test <- data.frame(Name=c("yoda","yoda","luke"),Value=c(1:3))
ggplot(test,aes(Name,Value,fill=Name)) + geom_bar(position="dodge")

So here I would like 3 bars under two labels.  Can this be done?

Thanks

How about...

test$fac<-c("a","b","a")
ggplot(test,aes(fac,Value)) + geom_bar(position="dodge")+ facet_grid(~Name, scales="free_x", space="free")

It's probably closer, but not really what you're asking for.

B

messages.subject: Re: "suppressing" x-axis / legend
messages.body_plain:
Hi, there's a typo in your code. It's legend.position not legeng_position. And + xlab("") should work to remove the x axis label.

dftest <- structure(list(date = structure(1:12, .Label = c("12.10.10",
"13.10.10", "14.10.10", "15.10.10", "16.10.10", "17.10.10",
"26.10.10",
"27.10.10", "28.10.10", "29.10.10", "30.10.10", "31.10.10"), class =
"factor"),
   group = c("MIC", "MIC", "MIC", "MIC", "MIC", "MIC", "SE",
   "SE", "SE", "SE", "SE", "SE"), value = c(0.2, 0.21, 0.22,
   0.23, 0.22, 0.23, 0.38, 0.39, 0.41, 0.43, 0.43, 0.42)), .Names =
c("date",
"group", "value"), row.names = c(NA, -12L), class = "data.frame")

p <- ggplot(dftest,aes(x=date,y=value,group=group,colour=group))
 p + geom_line(size=I(1.8)) +
scale_y_continuous("value",formatter="percent") +
scale_colour_hue("Group") + scale_x_discrete("Date")  +

opts(title="Title",legend.position="none") + xlab("")

HTH
Luciano

messages.subject: Re: geom_bar with multiple values for a category
messages.subject_clean: geom_bar with multiple values for a category
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

The only way it seems to me you could do something like that is to create unique values/levels for the names to render the plot and then change the labels of the bars on the x-axis and legend. Here are a couple of stabs at it, although I don't think either of these are what you really wanted. More on that below.

# (1): Create a new variable with unique names in each row.
#        In particular, I created a 'yoda' and a 'Yoda'. This will get
#        you three bars with individual counts represented, and
#        the labels can be adjusted with scale_* calls.

test <- data.frame(Name=c("yoda","yoda","luke"),Value=c(1:3))

test$Name2 <- as.character(test$Name)
test$Name2[2] <- 'Yoda'
> test
  Name Value Name2
1 yoda     1  yoda
2 yoda     2  Yoda
3 luke     3  luke

g <- ggplot(test, aes(x = Name2, fill = Name2))
g + geom_bar(aes(weight = Value)) + labs(fill = 'Name', x = 'Name') +
     scale_x_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name) +
     scale_fill_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name)

#--------
This gets you a chart with three bars, two names and three colors. Closer, but not what you wanted.
#--------

# (2) Use the original factor Name to supply the fill colors and Name2 to get individual bars per line.

h <- ggplot(test, aes(x = Name2, fill = Name))
h + geom_bar(aes(weight = Value), position = 'dodge') +
     labs(fill = 'Name', x = 'Name') +
     scale_x_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name) +
     scale_fill_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name)

I tried to use position = 'dodge' to get the two 'yoda' bars to hug each other, but to no avail. The 'good' news is that now yoda has a single color and a single representation in the legend - that's some progress, but it's still not what you wanted. The problem is that position = 'dodge' doesn't work because the bars are defined by the values of Name2, so they are in some sense considered 'independent' or 'ungrouped'. I don't see how you can get around that in ggplot2.

The problem is that you want to generate separate bars for individual lines in the data file, even if they have the same identifier (Name), but at the same time you want (a) bars with the same name grouped together under a single name, and  (b) presumably, bars with the same name to have the same color. You haven't supplied a sufficiently rich labeling mechanism to allow that to happen. With some work, you could do what you want in base graphics, but you'd have to set the following manually: the spacing between bars, the labels, the fill colors and the legend. Most of this you can do in the barplot() call; the bar labels would likely have to be set with axis(). If you have any familiarity with barplot(), I don't think it would be all that hard - you just have to read the help page carefully.

My guess is that if you stick with ggplot2, you may end up having to do something that combines what I did above with what Brandon showed you earlier by faceting. Unfortunately, I don't have a lot of time today to invest in this problem, so hopefully someone will provide a better answer.

HTH,
Dennis

test <- data.frame(Name=c("yoda","yoda","luke"),Value=c(1:3), g=1:3)

> > The only way it seems to me you could do something like that is to create
> > unique values/levels for the names to render the plot and then change the
> > labels of the bars on the x-axis and legend. Here are a couple of stabs at
> > it, although I don't think either of these are what you really wanted. More
> > on that below.
> >
> > # (1): Create a new variable with unique names in each row.
> > #        In particular, I created a 'yoda' and a 'Yoda'. This will get
> > #        you three bars with individual counts represented, and
> > #        the labels can be adjusted with scale_* calls.
> >
> > test <- data.frame(Name=c("yoda","yoda","luke"),Value=c(1:3))
> > test$Name2 <- as.character(test$Name)
> > test$Name2[2] <- 'Yoda'
> >> test
> >   Name Value Name2
> > 1 yoda     1  yoda
> > 2 yoda     2  Yoda
> > 3 luke     3  luke
> >
> > g <- ggplot(test, aes(x = Name2, fill = Name2))
> > g + geom_bar(aes(weight = Value)) + labs(fill = 'Name', x = 'Name') +
> >      scale_x_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name) +
> >      scale_fill_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name)
> >
> > #--------
> > This gets you a chart with three bars, two names and three colors. Closer,
> > but not what you wanted.
> > #--------
> >
> > # (2) Use the original factor Name to supply the fill colors and Name2 to
> > get individual bars per line.
> >
> > h <- ggplot(test, aes(x = Name2, fill = Name))
> > h + geom_bar(aes(weight = Value), position = 'dodge') +
> >      labs(fill = 'Name', x = 'Name') +
> >      scale_x_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name) +
> >      scale_fill_discrete(breaks = unique(test$Name2), labels = test$Name)
> >
> > I tried to use position = 'dodge' to get the two 'yoda' bars to hug each
> > other, but to no avail. The 'good' news is that now yoda has a single color
> > and a single representation in the legend - that's some progress, but it's
> > still not what you wanted. The problem is that position = 'dodge' doesn't
> > work because the bars are defined by the values of Name2, so they are in
> > some sense considered 'independent' or 'ungrouped'. I don't see how you can
> > get around that in ggplot2.
> >
> > The problem is that you want to generate separate bars for individual lines
> > in the data file, even if they have the same identifier (Name), but at the
> > same time you want (a) bars with the same name grouped together under a
> > single name, and  (b) presumably, bars with the same name to have the same
> > color. You haven't supplied a sufficiently rich labeling mechanism to allow
> > that to happen. With some work, you could do what you want in base graphics,
> > but you'd have to set the following manually: the spacing between bars, the
> > labels, the fill colors and the legend. Most of this you can do in the
> > barplot() call; the bar labels would likely have to be set with axis(). If
> > you have any familiarity with barplot(), I don't think it would be all that
> > hard - you just have to read the help page carefully.

> > My guess is that if you stick with ggplot2, you may end up having to do

messages.body_plain:
Hi Felipe:

On Thu, Jan 20, 2011 at 2:27 PM, Felipe Carrillo <mazatla...@yahoo.com> wrote:
> I figured out the bolditalic title problem, but now I am having problems with \n (newline). My X axis title
> is long and would like to write it on two different lines. How can I use \n inside the function "expression"

You can't; it's documented on the plotmath help page that
"Control characters (e.g. \n) are not interpreted in character strings in plotmath, unlike normal plotting."

I did some searching of the R-help archives but came up empty on finding a solution that produces multiline expressions in plot labels. Hopefully someone will have better luck.

A sleazy little trick for non-expressions is something like

... + xlabs('Here is a
two-line subtitle.')

but expressions are too smart to be fooled by that ruse..I tried. Evidently, you need a cleverer trick :)

Maybe you can figure out how to do something along the lines of Marc Schwartz's suggestion in the following R-help post:
http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/Plotmath-and-line-breaks-in-long-annotations-for-plots-td880718.html#a880719

The use of do.call(expression, ...) sounds like it might have some promise. The problem is that the solution is for text() in base graphics; you'd have to figure out how to translate to an equivalent in xlabs() or scale_*.

When someone figures this out, please post it; I'd be interested in the solution.

Hope this is of some help,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: partial italic axis titles
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You could hack opts() with a custom grob for the x axis title,

library(ggplot2)

my.title = function(...) {
  g1 <- textGrob(expression(bold("first line")),
                 0.5, 1, hjust = 0.5, vjust = 2)
  g2 <- textGrob(expression(italic("second line")), 0.5, 0,
                 hjust = 0.5, vjust = 3)
  gTree(children=gList(g1, g2))

}

qplot(1,1, geom="blank") + opts(axis.title.x = my.title,
             plot.margin = unit(c(1,1,3,1), "lines"))

HTH,

baptiste

help from gridExtra,

library(gridExtra)

my.title = function(expressions) {
  function(...)
    tableGrob(expressions, parse=TRUE,
              theme=theme.list(gpar.corefill = gpar(fill = NA, col = NA),
                core.just = "center"))
}

e = expression(alpha,"testing", italic(italic),
    hat(beta), integral(f(x)*dx, a, b))

qplot(1,1, geom="blank") + opts(axis.title.x = my.title(e))

HTH,

baptiste

messages.body_plain:
Hi -

In Hadley's book there is the standard example. (~p.153)
The following isnt comprehensive (since it's not reproducible), but I believe you'll be able to make sense of it (and in the doc i was currently working on). Note that you can also use ranges in vplayout, eg vplayout(1,2:3). Also i've left ggplot() to mean whatever you need to plot, not an actual command, since i'm not using any supplied data.

---------------------------
vplayout <- function(x,y)
  viewport(layout.pos.row=x,layout.pos.col=y)

overall <- ggplot( )
ts.fraction <- ggplot( )
continent.fraction <- ggplot()
duration.fraction <- ggplot()
area.fraction <- ggplot( )
magnitude.fraction <- ggplot()

pdf('heavy_rain_floods.pdf',width=11,height=8.5)
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(3,2)))

print(overall,vp=vplayout(1,1))
print(ts.fraction, vp=vplayout(1,2))
print(continent.fraction, vp=vplayout(2,1))
print(duration.fraction, vp=vplayout(2,2))
print(area.fraction, vp=vplayout(3,1))
print(magnitude.fraction, vp=vplayout(3,2))

dev.off()

Best,

James

messages.body_plain:
Another option may be to use the function 'arrange' below. For example,

myplot1 <- ggplot(dataframe,aes(x=variable,=y=variable)) + geom_point()
myplot2 <- ggplot(dataframe,aes(x=variable,=y=variable)) + geom_point()
arrange(myplot1,myplot2,ncol=1) # you can specify ncol and nrow as well

# Function used below in the function 'arrange'

vp.layout <- function(x, y) viewport(layout.pos.row=x, layout.pos.col=y)

# Function to plot multiple ggplots together

arrange <- function(..., nrow=NULL, ncol=NULL, as.table=FALSE) {

 dots <- list(...)

 n <- length(dots)

 if(is.null(nrow) & is.null(ncol)) { nrow = floor(n/2) ; ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)}

 if(is.null(nrow)) { nrow = ceiling(n/ncol)}

 if(is.null(ncol)) { ncol = ceiling(n/nrow)}

        ## NOTE see n2mfrow in grDevices for possible alternative

grid.newpage()

pushViewport(viewport(layout=grid.layout(nrow,ncol) ) )

 ii.p <- 1

 for(ii.row in seq(1, nrow)){

 ii.table.row <- ii.row

 if(as.table) {ii.table.row <- nrow - ii.table.row + 1}

  for(ii.col in seq(1, ncol)){

   ii.table <- ii.p

   if(ii.p > n) break

   print(dots[[ii.table]], vp=vp.layout(ii.table.row, ii.col))

   ii.p <- ii.p + 1

  }

 }

}

SAC

messages.subject: Re: Comprehensive Example of using grid to show multiple plots in one graphic
messages.subject_clean: Comprehensive Example of using grid to show multiple plots in one graphic
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

There was a thread last spring that concerned this topic. Here's an example I drummed up at the time; the idea was to use theme_blank() to remove the plot.background. I also messed around with the viewport centers manually. See below for another approach.

# Generate a Brownian motion series
df <- data.frame(t = 1:1000, y = cumsum(rnorm(1000)))
rg <- range(df$y)
fn <- function(x) ifelse(x < 0, floor(x), ceiling(x))
rg <- sapply(rg, fn)

# Idea is a time series plot with a rotated histogram next to it
# p is the time series plot, q is the rotated histogram
# in q, cut out the xlab and value labels
p <- qplot(x = t, y = y, data = df) + ylim(rg[1], rg[2])
q <- qplot(x = y, data = df) + coord_flip() +
           xlim(rg[1], rg[2]) +
           opts(axis.text.y = theme_blank()) + xlab('')

# strip off the plot backgrounds to pull plots closer together
p2 <- p + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())
q2 <- q + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())

# Create some viewports
vp2 <- viewport(width = 0.25, height = 1, x = 0.875, y = 0.5)
vp3 <- viewport(width = 0.85, height = 1, x = 0.425, y = 0.5)

# The first pair of plots has overrunning space; the second
# pair does not. The x11() window works on my Win7 box;
# if it doesn't work, try another device.

x11(7, 3.5)
print(q, vp = vp2)
print(p, vp = vp3)

grid.newpage()
print(q2, vp = vp2)
print(p2, vp = vp3)
dev.off()
#------------------------

Fernando also contributed to that thread, and his approach used plot.margin instead. This is the part I kept, so some context may be lost:

######### Fernando's example using opts(plot.margin) ##########

p <- q <- qplot(1, 1) + opts(plot.background = theme_blank())

# View graphs before the margins are altered
grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1, 2)))
print(p, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(q, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))

# left margin negative compensated with a larger right margin
# to maintain the proportions of the plot [aspect ratio]
q <- q + opts(plot.margin = unit(c(1, 3, 0.5, -2.5), "lines"))

grid.newpage()
pushViewport(viewport(layout = grid.layout(1, 2)))
print(p, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(q, vp = viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))

Fernando's method is more robust than mine, since it fine tunes the parameters rather than hunting and pecking to fit.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.subject: Re: partial italic axis titles
messages.body_plain:
The tableGrob approach has the advantage of being more versatile
(arbitrary number of rows, automatic line spacing), and doesn't
require to manually adjust the ggplot plot margins,

library(gridExtra)

my.title = function(expressions) {
  function(...)
    tableGrob(matrix(expressions), parse=TRUE,
              theme=theme.list(gpar.corefill = gpar(fill = NA, col = NA),
                core.just = "center"))
}

title <- expression(paste("Figure 20. Actual passage of Pacific

species ", italic("Penaeus vannamei"),

    " migrating to the San Francisco Bay"), italic("second line"))

qplot(1,1, geom="blank") + opts(axis.title.x = my.title(title))

That said, I would personally place the figure title outside of the
plot, not in the axis label,

library(gridExtra)

p <- qplot(1,1, geom="blank") + xlab("")

caption <- tableGrob(matrix(expression(paste("Figure 20. Actual

passage of Pacific species ", italic("Penaeus vannamei"),

    " migrating to the San Francisco Bay"), italic("second line"))),

                     parse=TRUE, theme=theme.list(gpar.corefill =
gpar(fill = NA, col = NA),
                                   core.just = "center"))

grid.arrange(p,  sub=caption)

HTH,

baptiste

require to manually adjust the ggplot plot margins,

messages.subject_clean: geom_smooth error when faceting on variable called "start"
messages.body_plain:
This is curious. The following code runs fine for me:

set.seed(123)
dat <-
data.frame(x=runif(200),y=runif(200),strt=rep(c('A','B','C','D'),times=25))
ggplot(dat,aes(x=x,y=y)) +
	geom_point() +
	facet_wrap(~strt) +
	geom_smooth()

However, this produces an error:

set.seed(123)
dat <-
data.frame(x=runif(200),y=runif(200),start=rep(c('A','B','C','D'),times=25))
ggplot(dat,aes(x=x,y=y)) +
	geom_point() +
	facet_wrap(~start) +
	geom_smooth()

Specifically: "Error in grid.Call.graphics("L_lines", x$x, x$y, index,
x$arrow) :
  invalid line type"

Now that I've figured it out, it's easy enough not to call my
variables "start", but I thought I'd share in case this snagged anyone
else.

messages.subject: Re: pattern fill
messages.body_plain:
Flicking through the pgf manual, there is now a rather nice collection
of built-in patterns. I believe this is the way to go; patterns should
be implemented at a low level (e.g. by the graphics device), because
they require costly/painful calculations of intersections and tiling.
Perhaps the tikzDevice or the Cairo device could be adapted to allow
this? Ideally Grid's gpar() would be modified too, to pass a pattern
to devices that support it.

baptiste

> could use it to pattern over an area of a map. I see its' main purpose as
> making graph objects distinctive in the absence of color or over the top of
> color. I would suggest that is perhaps it's sole purpose (primarily for
> publication reasons), although I'm sure others could come up with other
> reasons it could be useful to them.

messages.body_plain:
I've been building this function which takes a large table of data and plots histograms, scatterplots, a correlation matrix, runs a PCA, plots biplots, score plots and loadings plots, and finally plots the R2VX of the PCA model. It's a bit overgrown and written by a physiologist, but I have this problem which is confusing me.

The function call looks like this:
Comboplotter(filename="/Users/brandonhurr/Desktop/Laurent Analysis/Practice Tomato Data/tomato.dataw-outNAs.txt", colstart=3, standard.names=c("2421-1-M:99-B-2-B-"), start.nPCs= 15, text.labels=c("Abbrcd"), mol.type.file="/Users/brandonhurr/Desktop/Laurent Analysis/Practice Tomato Data/tomato.mol.typew-outNAs.txt", cor.limit=0.8, pval.limit=0.001)

When I run it, I get this error.
[1] "YOU HAVE SUPPLIED A TAB DELIMITED TEXT FILE FOR ANALYSIS"
[1] "THE FOLLOWING ROWS HAVE INCOMPLETE DATA THAT WILL BE REMOVED BEFORE ANALYSIS"
[1] "160"
[1] "SUPPLIED VARIABLES ARE NUMERIC, PROCEEDING WITH CALCULATIONS"
[1] "STANDARD 2421-1-M:99-B-2-B- FOUND."
[1] "FACTOR FOR TEXT LABELS Abbrcd FOUND."
[1] "REPLICATION UNDEFINED, NOT COMPUTING AVERAGES"
Error in paste(standard.names) : object 'standard.names' not found

Which I isolated to this bit of code (Full code attached).

#Density/Distribution plot

if (length(standard.names) == 1){

melon.data.standard.avg<- ddply(melon.data.standard, paste(colnames(melon.data)[fac.pos]), colwise(mean))

# droplevels to get rid of excess factor levels for plotting

melon.data.standard.avg<-droplevels(melon.data.standard.avg)

for (i in colstart:colend){

plot<-ggplot()+

geom_histogram(data=melon.data, aes_string(x= paste(colnames(melon.data)[i])))+

geom_vline(data=melon.data.standard.avg, aes_string(xintercept= paste(colnames(melon.data)[i])), colour= "lightblue3")+

theme_bw()+

geom_text(data=melon.data.standard.avg, aes_string(x=paste(colnames(melon.data)[i]), y= "0", label='paste(standard.names)') , angle=90, colour="lightblue3", hjust=0, vjust=0, size=3)

#save plot

ggsave(sprintf("Histogram.%s.%s.%s.png", (i-colstart+1), mol.type$mol.type[(i-colstart+1)], colnames(melon.data)[i]), width=6, height=6)

}

}

standard.names is used to ID standards and mark them on the distribution plot. If I make standard.names longer than 2 it works beautifully, but in a slightly different way. If there are no standards it works great, but I needed to account for only having one standard. When I run this code out of the function, it works. When I run the function with standard.names defined in the global space it works, but when I run it in the function it fails with the above error.

Does anyone have a clue what is going on because I am truly at a loss?

Brandon

Thanks anyone in advance for your help.

Adam Loveland

ggplot2 isn't really set up to do this (there is no scale_numeric as

ggplot(tst,aes(x,y))+geom_point()+geom_text(aes(label=desc),size=3,vjust=-1)

don't know if you can get it to really look right.

Best,
Ista

messages.subject: Re: aes(size=levels(factor))
messages.body_plain:
I don't think it possible just with ggplot.  The closest you can get
is setting the legend.key option in the theme, but this just controls
the decoration around the displayed point.  In particular, setting it
to theme_blank() does not suppress the key itself, just any decoration
around it.

If you know enough about grid graphics, it should be possible to go
back after the plot is made and change the underlying grid structure
to eliminate those grobs.  I don't know grid well enough to say how to
do this, though.

--
Brian S. Diggs, PhD
Senior Research Associate, Department of Surgery
Oregon Health & Science University
